Assume Countable Choice. Let $G$ be an oriented knot grid of size $n\ge2$, with its actual flat torus and product generator end charts. Write $M_O,M_X$ and $A_G=(M_O-M_X)/2-(n-1)/2$ for the grid grading functions. For every actual continuous Whitney class $\phi:x\to y$ in $\operatorname{Sym}^n(T)$, define its domain and marked multiplicities by the relative point-divisor degrees of any smooth model. Its actual fixed-end Fredholm index $\mu(\phi)$, before source translation, satisfies
$$\mu(\phi)=M_O(x)-M_O(y)+2\sum_{i=1}^n n_{O_i}(\phi),$$
and
$$A_G(x)-A_G(y)=\sum_{i=1}^n n_{X_i}(\phi)-\sum_{i=1}^n n_{O_i}(\phi).$$
These identities hold for all realized classes, with positive, zero or negative marked multiplicities. In particular no condition $n_X=0$ is imposed. They remain valid for the actual linearized index of a smooth finite-energy holomorphic strip with generator ends and the protected product end data, under the auxiliary complex-structure homotopies in the suppliers.

Consequently, an actual index-one holomorphic strip counted with weight $\prod_i U_i^{n_{O_i}}$, if all its marked multiplicities are nonnegative, lowers $M_O$ by one and drops the $A_G$ filtration by exactly $\sum_i n_{X_i}$, when $U_i$ has bidegree $(-2,-1)$. This is the full filtered relative grading assertion, rather than only its zero-$X$ associated graded specialization. It does not assert existence or finiteness of counts, square-zero, move invariance, a grid-to-analytic equivalence, or identification of an absolute analytic grading normalization.

Assume Countable Choice. Use a size-$n\ge2$ toroidal grid, its flat oriented torus $T=\mathbb R^2/(n\mathbb Z)^2$, horizontal alpha circles and vertical beta circles, and $X=\operatorname{Sym}^n(T)$. At each generator use the actual flat product chart with alpha plane $\mathbb R^n$ and beta plane $i\mathbb R^n$. The path of target almost complex structures may be any homotopy of the standard complex structure compatible with these boundary planes and fixed product ends as in the relative-index suppliers.

For each embedded grid rectangle $R$ from $x$ to $y$, with $x$ at its northeast and southwest corners and with no other point of $x$ in its interior, there is an actual continuous Whitney class $r_R:x\to y$ whose domain is exactly $R$ and whose actual fixed-end Fredholm index is $1$. Markings inside $R$ are unrestricted.

For every generator $x$ and every closed band between consecutive horizontal grid circles there is an actual based disk on $L_\alpha$, based at $x$, with domain that unit row annulus and boundary Maslov index $2$. Likewise every consecutive column annulus is the domain of an actual based disk on $L_\beta$ with boundary Maslov index $2$. Inserting either disk on the corresponding boundary of the constant Whitney class at $x$ gives a class $x\to x$ of actual fixed-end index $2$. Reversals give the negative domains and negative indices, and finite concatenations are actual classes with additive domains and indices.

All these assertions construct classes and compute their linearized indices. They do not count holomorphic representatives, prove moduli regularity, or identify absolute gradings or an analytic invariant.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a closed oriented Riemann surface with an actual finite oriented polygon as in the sphere-index theorem, $m\ge1$, and put $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma)$. Let $\boldsymbol\alpha,\boldsymbol\beta$ be two disjoint-within-system smooth curve families of size $m$, transverse to each other, with product tori $L_\alpha,L_\beta$. Give two smooth fixed-end Whitney disk models $u,v$ from the same generator $x$ to the same generator $y$, constant near their two marked boundary corners, with their actual fixed product end data. Use the auxiliary complex-structure homotopies and actual relative-index realizations specified in the relative Whitney index theorem. Domain coefficients mean the integer relative degrees of the point-divisor lines, not a holomorphic representative assumption.

For any such pair, $D(u)-D(v)$ has boundary a sum of full attaching circles. The coefficient on each oriented circle is the angular winding difference of the corresponding labelled boundary paths, with their source-boundary signs. In particular, if $D(u)=D(v)$ as region chains, their boundary paths on each labelled alpha circle are homotopic relative their endpoints, and likewise on each labelled beta circle. After these boundary homotopies the difference of their smooth relative classes is represented by a sphere $A$ with $n_z(A)=0$. Consequently
$$\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb R}(u)=\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb R}(v),$$
before source translation, on all the stated higher Sobolev and allowed smooth weighted realizations. Thus actual Fredholm index is well defined on the set of REALIZED Whitney domains, including classes with positive, zero or negative marked multiplicities. No assertion that every integer region chain is realized is made.

The analogous statement holds for two smooth disks based at the same point of a single product torus $L_\gamma$, with equal one-system domains: their boundary loops are based homotopic, and their boundary Maslov indices and compact-disk Fredholm indices agree. Their fixed-node indices also agree whenever that bounded point-trace realization is used. The finite polygon hypothesis is supplied for the original embedded balanced $S^3$ data by the broad-input application in the sphere-index theorem. No full formula $e(D)+n_x(D)+n_y(D)$, normalized relative or absolute grading, invariance, or arbitrary-domain representativity is included.

Let $M^n$ be an oriented smooth manifold without boundary. For each compact set $K\subseteq M$ there are finitely many nonnegative smooth functions $\chi_i$ with compact supports contained in connected coordinate domains $U_i$, such that $\sum_i\chi_i=1$ on a neighbourhood of $K$. For $\omega\in\Omega_c^n(M)$ define
$$\mathcal I_M(\omega)=\sum_i I_{\phi_i}(\chi_i\omega)\quad(K=\operatorname{supp}\omega),$$
using the signed chart integrals. This value is independent of the finite functions and charts. It defines a linear functional, is local under restriction to an open set containing the support, and for $n\ge1$ satisfies
$$\mathcal I_M(d\eta)=0\qquad(\eta\in\Omega_c^{n-1}(M)).$$
For $n=0$ it is the finite signed sum $\sum_{p\in\operatorname{supp}\omega}\varepsilon(p)\omega(p)$. All assertions are choice-free: no partition on the entire manifold is required.

derivations.claim: Number cells by $(i,j)\in(\mathbb Z/n)^2$, with cell $D_{ij}$ northeast of vertex $(i,j)$. Define the vertex functions $$\Delta D_{ij}=D_{ij}+D_{i-1,j-1}-D_{i-1,j}-D_{i,j-1},\qquad QD_{ij}=\tfrac14(D_{ij}+D_{i-1,j-1}+D_{i-1,j}+D_{i,j-1}).$$ For the actual domain one has $\Delta D=1_x-1_y$. Here is the local boundary verification. By [F2], the jump across each open alpha edge counts its actual labelled boundary path with sign. At an alpha-beta crossing its change from the preceding to the succeeding edge is the endpoint coefficient of that path, namely one at its source state point and minus one at its target state point. The alternating four cell sum displayed above is exactly that change, with the grid orientation in which a rectangle has its source at southwest/northeast. Common state points cancel. Full-circle winding terms are constant on the circle and introduce no change. Equivalently apply [F2]'s ordered-root Stokes calculation on the four edges of a small crossing neighborhood; each labelled path appears with its actual degree, so division by the finite ordered-cover degree gives this same endpoint coefficient. Thus the assertion holds for signed degrees as well as positive ones. Also $QD=\nu(D)$ by definition. [F2, given, construct, algebra]

The finite pairing $\langle\Delta E,QD\rangle$ is symmetric in $D,E$. To check this without a boundary term, let $S_i,S_j$ be the backward cyclic shifts on cell arrays. Then $\Delta=(1-S_i)(1-S_j)$, $Q=(1+S_i)(1+S_j)/4$, and, for the ordinary finite sum pairing, $S_i^*=S_i^{-1}$ and $S_j^*=S_j^{-1}$. All shifts commute. Hence $$\Delta^*Q=\tfrac14(S_i-S_i^{-1})(S_j-S_j^{-1})$$ is self-adjoint: transposing changes the sign of each of its two factors. This proves the stated symmetry by a finite matrix identity, including cells crossing either chosen seam. No fundamental-square pair-count convention is needed here. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

For a domain $D:x\to y$ put $F_{xy}(D)=\langle1_x+1_y,QD\rangle$. If $E:y\to z$, step 1.1 and step 2.1 give $$F_{xz}(D+E)-F_{xy}(D)-F_{yz}(E)=\langle1_z-1_y,QD\rangle+\langle1_x-1_y,QE\rangle=-\langle\Delta E,QD\rangle+\langle\Delta D,QE\rangle=0.$$ It negates under endpoint reversal and domain negation. On an empty-state rectangle, its four changed corner measures are $1/4$ each, and all common state measures vanish, so $F=1$. On a unit row annulus loop, exactly two state points are on its bounding horizontal circles, each of measure $1/2$; all others have measure zero. Thus $F_{xx}=2n_x=2$. A column annulus has the same count on its two bounding vertical circles. For $n=2$ these two circles are still distinct and the same calculation applies. By [F1] concatenate these actual models to match $D$, using signs for negative annuli. Additivity makes $F_{xy}(D)$ equal their actual index sum; equal-domain index comparison in [F1] identifies this sum with $\mu(u)$. This proves the all-realized-class point-measure formula. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

Assume now $D\ge0$ and $\mu=1$. If $x=y$, the last formula in [F1] makes its index the even integer $2\sum n_O$, impossible. Otherwise let $r$ be the number of points of $x$ not in $y$. The state-permutation condition gives $r\ge2$: changing exactly one point cannot preserve both its row and column. There are $2r$ changed vertices. At each, $|\Delta D|=1$ by step 1.1. Since its four coefficients are nonnegative integers, their sum is at least one, so its point measure is at least $1/4$. Common vertices have nonnegative measure and occur twice in $n_x+n_y$. Thus step 3.1 gives $1\ge r/2$, forcing $r=2$. Equality forces precisely one adjacent cell coefficient one and the other three zero at every changed vertex, and all four coefficients zero at every common vertex. In particular all changed corners are convex, with no reflex or higher-multiplicity alternative. [F1, step 1.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

Only the two changed rows and two changed columns can support the chain boundary of $D$. On any other horizontal circle its jump is constant between crossings, by step 1.1, since there is no changed endpoint on that circle; at its common state point both adjacent coefficients vanish by step 4.1, so the jump is zero everywhere. The same holds for any other vertical circle. On each changed row, its two changed vertices divide it into two proper cyclic arcs. The jump is constant on each open arc; the one-positive-quadrant pattern at either endpoint says one arc has jump of magnitude one and the other zero. The same conclusion holds on each changed column. Thus the entire boundary consists of four oriented arcs connecting those four vertices, one on each changed circle, each of multiplicity one. They form one four-edge cycle: every vertex has one horizontal and one vertical incident arc and the rows and columns are distinct. Since this is the boundary of the actual torus cell chain, its integrals against the global closed forms $dx,dy$ vanish by [F3]. The two horizontal arcs therefore have opposite signed displacements of the same magnitude, so they select the same proper column interval in opposite directions. The vertical arcs likewise select the same proper row interval. Consequently this cycle is the boundary of the embedded product of those two intervals, a torus rectangle $R$. The positive-quadrant pattern fixes the boundary sign as $+\partial R$, rather than its negative: the latter would have three positive adjacent quadrants after adding a constant, not exactly one. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

Now $\partial(D-R)=0$. Across each grid edge its two coefficients agree, so the connected rectangular torus grid makes $D-R$ a constant multiple of the whole torus. At a changed corner the three exterior coefficients of $D$ and of $R$ are all zero; hence that constant is zero and $D=R$. All common state point measures vanish by step 4.1, so no common point lies inside $R$. Its only remaining state points are its two source and two target corners. Finally $\Delta R=1_x-1_y$ fixes which alternating corners are the source; this is exactly the oriented rectangle convention. Marks were never restricted, and their positive degrees remain allowed. This completes only the stated index and positive-domain classification. [step 1.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

Steps 4.1 through 6.1 classify nonnegative actual index1 domains.
Steps 1.1 through 3.1 retain all signed domains, seams and n2 annuli.
Step 1.1 identifies the actual endpoint corner stencil, including common points.
Steps 1.1 through 6.1 use finite arrays, actual models and finite cell boundary arguments.
